text: Get a warrant. Three words from the Supreme Court, and everyone stopped reading there.
provenance: The ruling came down to three words that are now quoted constantly: get a warrant

text: The Court did not say police can never see what is on your phone. It said they have to go to a judge, show probable cause, and get one.
provenance: The Court did not say the police can never see what is on your phone. It said they have to do what the Constitution normally requires for something this private: go to a judge, show probable cause, and get a warrant

text: And it left a door open. In a true emergency, a bomb, a kidnapping, a child in danger, police can still act without waiting. It protects your phone. It does not make it a shield.
provenance: The Court left one important door open. In a true emergency — a bomb, a kidnapping, a child in danger — the police can still act without waiting for a warrant

text: Then look at what it actually guarded. The messages, the photos, the files you put there on purpose. Not what your phone creates on its own and hands to your carrier.
provenance: It protects the contents of the phone — the messages, the photos, the files you can see when you unlock it. It assumes the private thing is the data you put there on purpose.
Every few minutes, it tells the nearest tower where it is.

text: You never type that trail. You never see it. And almost nobody read far enough into the ruling to find out who owns it.
